exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Ruth. It tells us that, in the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land of Israel. Because of this, a man from Bethlehem in Judah went to live as a foreigner in the country of Moab, together with his wife and his two sons. Living as a foreigner here means staying for a time in a land that is not one's own.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who does not identify himself; we do not know for certain who wrote it. He sets the story in the time of the judges, a period that other books describe as difficult and marked by little faithfulness to God. The family does not leave out of whim, but in search of survival. Moab was a neighboring people, and relations between Moab and Israel were often strained.

For today: when seasons of scarcity or uncertainty come, we can ask God for wisdom in our decisions and trust that He cares for us, even on unexpected paths.
exp.0:1:
The verse introduces a family from Bethlehem: Elimelech, his wife Naomi, and their sons Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites, that is, from the region of Ephrath, where Bethlehem is located. Because of the famine, they went to Moab and continued living there.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who tells a story from the time of the judges. He gives names and places to show that these are real people. The author does not name himself, and it is not known for certain who he was. The family left out of necessity, and what was meant to be a temporary stay gradually grew longer.

Today, when a crisis comes, we can pray and ask God for direction before deciding, so that an emergency exit does not become a course we never intended to take.
exp.0:6:
This verse tells that Naomi left the place where she had lived in Moab. Her two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, went out with her, and the three of them began to walk back toward the land of Judah.

The narrator describes the moment when Naomi, a widow without sons, decides to return to her homeland. She had heard that the Lord had visited his people by giving them bread, that is, that the famine had ended. After losing her husband and her two sons, returning was her best option for survival.

For today: when life leaves us wounded and without direction, sometimes the first step is simply to return toward where we know God is at work. We do not need to have everything resolved; it is enough to begin walking toward him.
exp.0:7:
Naomi tells her two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, to go back, each one to her mother's house. She wishes that the Lord may show kindness to them, meaning faithful love and goodness, just as they showed it to their husbands who died and to her.

Naomi is a widow who lost her husband and her two sons in Moab. Hearing that the Lord had given bread to Judah, she decides to return to her homeland. Thinking about the future of the young women, who are also widows, she asks them to stay in their own land, where they could start their lives again and have a home.

For today: we can learn from Naomi to bless others even when we ourselves are suffering. Think of someone close to you and ask God to take care of them, or speak a sincere word of encouragement to them.
exp.0:8:
Naomi wishes her daughters-in-law that the Lord would grant them rest, that is, security and stability, each one in the house of a new husband. Then she kisses them, and they weep aloud.

Naomi is speaking. She is a widow who lost her husband and her two sons in Moab, and now she is returning to Judah. Her daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, are Moabites. She blesses them and encourages them to stay in their own land, thinking of their well-being, even though that means being left alone.

Today we can learn to bless others sincerely, even when parting hurts us. Loving someone truly is sometimes wanting the best for them, even if that person no longer stays by our side. We can pray for those who go away and entrust them to God.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that Orpah and Ruth, Naomi's two daughters-in-law, answer her together: "Surely we will return with you to your people." They reject the idea of going back to their families and want to accompany Naomi.

Naomi is an Israelite widow who is going back to Judah after losing her husband and her two sons in Moab. She asks her daughters-in-law to stay in their land and look for a new home. The young women weep and, out of love, insist on going with her. Later Naomi insists again, and it will be seen that each one makes a different decision.

For today: true love shows itself by standing with someone in their pain. Today you can do the same with a relative or friend who is suffering: stay by their side, listen to them, and help them faithfully, without waiting until you have all the answers.
exp.0:11:
Naomi asks her daughters-in-law to turn back to their own land. She tells them she is too old to marry again. And she adds, as a supposition, that even if she had hope of having a husband that very night and bore sons, that would change nothing.

Naomi speaks; she is an Israelite widow who lost her husband and her two sons in Moab. Orpah and Ruth, her daughters-in-law, are also widows and want to accompany her to Bethlehem. Naomi is in grief and thinks of their good. She shows them that she can no longer give them a future. Some understand her words as generous love, and others also see in them her bitterness.

For today: when someone suffers, they can think clearly and lovingly about the good of others. But we can also remember that God continues to work even when our strength and hopes seem exhausted.
exp.0:12:
Naomi asks her daughters-in-law two questions: would they wait for sons who were not yet born to grow up? Would they stay unmarried for that reason? She answers her own questions: no. Naomi says her bitterness is greater than theirs, because she feels that the hand of the Lord has gone out against her.

Naomi speaks as a widow who lost her husband and her two sons in Moab. Here she tries to persuade Orpah and Ruth to go back to their families. According to the custom of the time, a brother-in-law could marry a widow, but Naomi no longer had any more sons. Her grief leads her to believe that God is against her, though this is how she feels it and not the final word of the book.

For today: when you suffer, you can be honest with God, as Naomi was. But do not judge your whole story by your present pain; God may be at work even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.0:13:
This verse tells how Naomi and her two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, wept aloud once more. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye and went back home, but Ruth stayed close to Naomi.

Naomi was a widow, and she had also lost her two sons in Moab. She decided to return to Bethlehem and tried to persuade her daughters-in-law to stay in their own land, where they could marry again. Orpah did what seemed sensible; Ruth chose loyalty. The text does not condemn Orpah, it simply shows the contrast between the two.

For today: there are hard decisions where the most comfortable choice is to step away. Ruth invites us to be faithful to people who are suffering, standing with them in love, even when it costs us. Today you can call or visit someone going through a hard time and stay by their side.
exp.0:15:
Ruth tells Naomi not to press her to leave her or to turn back from following her. She promises to go wherever Naomi goes and to stay wherever Naomi stays. She also declares that Naomi's people will be her people and that Naomi's God will be her God.

Naomi is an Israelite widow who returns to Bethlehem after losing her husband and her two sons in Moab. Ruth, a Moabite and the widow of one of her sons, could have gone back to her own family, as Orpah did. Naomi advises her to do so out of affection, but Ruth decides to stay. Her words express loyalty and faith, because she chooses the God of Israel as well.

For today: loyalty is shown through actions, especially when accompanying someone costs something. Think of a person going through a difficult time and look for one concrete way to stand beside them this week.
exp.0:21:
This verse says that Naomi returned to Bethlehem together with Ruth, her daughter-in-law from Moab. They came back from the country of Moab just as the barley harvest was beginning.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Naomi had just told the women of Bethlehem about her grief: she had lost her husband and her two sons, and she felt empty and bitter. But the verse mentions Ruth at her side and the start of the harvest. Without saying it in words, the account lets us see that the story does not end in bitterness. Later we will see how God cares for them.

For today: even when you feel empty or hurt, be honest with God and do not turn away from Him. Notice also the people He has placed beside you, and the small beginnings of hope.
exp.1:6:
The overseer of the harvesters is telling Boaz what Ruth asked for. She begged to be allowed to glean and gather grain behind the reapers, among the sheaves. From morning until now she has been working, and she rested only briefly in the house, that is, in a shelter or hut in the field.

The one speaking is the servant in charge of the harvesters. Boaz had just asked who this young woman was. Ruth was a Moabite widow who had come back with Naomi. The law of Moses allowed the poor and foreigners to gather what was left in the fields. The servant points out her humility, since she asked for permission, and her steadiness. Afterward Boaz looks after her and gives her protection.

For today: humility and steady work open doors. Do faithfully what is in front of you, without complaining, and trust that God can use others to care for you.
exp.1:8:
Boaz tells Ruth to keep her eyes on the field where the reapers are harvesting and to follow after the women who are working there. He has commanded the young men, the workers, not to bother her. If she is thirsty, she may go to the jars and drink from the water the young men have drawn.

The speaker is Boaz, a landowner and relative of Naomi. Ruth is a foreign widow who gathers the leftover grain, something the law of Israel allowed the poor to do. Boaz had already heard about her loyalty to her mother-in-law and wants to protect her and give her a secure source of provision.

Today we can imitate Boaz by caring for those who are vulnerable: an immigrant, a widow, or a new colleague. A simple act, such as offering protection, help, or a cup of water, can reflect God's care.
exp.1:10:
Boaz answers Ruth that he has already heard all that she has done for her mother-in-law, Naomi, after her husband died. He tells her that she left her father, her mother, and the land where she was born, and came to live among a people she did not know before.

Ruth, a young widow from Moab, asked Boaz why he was treating her with such kindness when she was a foreigner. Boaz, a respected man of Bethlehem, replies that her reputation has gone ahead of her. He has seen her loyalty and self-sacrifice toward Naomi, and for that reason he cares for her and protects her in the field.

For today: God sees and values acts of love and faithfulness that no one applauds. Keep caring for your family and remaining loyal, even when it costs you, because God uses people who notice, and those people may bless you.
exp.1:12:
Ruth answers Boaz with humility. She asks to go on finding favor in his eyes, because he has comforted her and has spoken kindly to her heart.

Ruth herself is the one speaking, and the people she calls servants are Boaz's workers. She recognizes that she does not even have the place of one of them.

Ruth is a young widow from Moab who left her homeland to accompany Naomi, her mother-in-law, in Bethlehem. Boaz, the owner of the field, has just praised her loyalty and blessed her. She is surprised by such kindness, being a foreigner and poor. Then Boaz invites her to eat with him.

For today: a kind word can lift up someone who feels out of place. Today you can notice a new person, someone alone or in need, and encourage them with sincere words. And if you receive comfort, thank the one who gave it with humility.
exp.1:13:
At mealtime, Boaz told her to come over, to eat the bread and dip it in the vinegar. She sat beside the reapers, and he passed her roasted grain. Ruth ate until she was satisfied and still had some left over. The "vinegar" was probably a sour drink or sauce for dipping the bread.

Boaz is the owner of the field, and Ruth is a foreign widow from Moab who gathers grain to support her mother-in-law Naomi. Just before this, Boaz had recognized her loyalty and wished her God's protection. Now he backs up those words with action: not only words, but a place at the table, a seat, and food. In this way he treats her as someone welcome and not as a stranger.

For today: when you bless someone, do not stop at good words. Look at what you can offer, such as food, company, or a place, so that they feel accepted.
exp.1:14:
It says that Ruth got up to keep gleaning, that is, gathering the ears of grain left in the field after the harvest. Then Boaz ordered his servants (his workers) to let her gather grain even among the sheaves, which are the bundles of barley already tied, and not to shame her, that is, not to humiliate her or treat her with contempt.

Ruth was a widow from Moab who had come to Bethlehem with her mother-in-law Naomi. Boaz, the owner of the field, had already comforted her and given her food. Now he goes further than what the law required for the poor: he opens a larger door for her and protects her dignity before the other workers.

For today: when we help someone in need, it is not enough to give them something. Let us also take care of their dignity, treating them with respect and without making them feel lesser.
exp.1:17:
This verse tells how Ruth carried the barley she had gathered and went back to the town. Her mother-in-law Naomi saw how much she had collected. Then Ruth also took out the food that was left over after she had eaten her fill, and gave it to Naomi. Here "gleaned" means gathering up grain, and gleaning is picking up the ears of grain left behind in the field.

Ruth, a foreign widow, has spent the day working in Boaz's field, and Boaz had ordered that she be allowed to gather grain without being mistreated. The narrator shows that she kept nothing for herself: she shared with Naomi, who was also a widow and was in need. Afterward, Naomi will ask her where she worked.

For today: when God gives us something good, we can think about who else needs it. Sharing what we have left over, or what we have, is a simple way to show love and gratitude.
exp.1:19:
Naomi blesses Boaz when she learns his name. She says that God has not stopped showing kindness to the living or to the dead. Then she explains that Boaz is a relative of theirs and one of their close kinsmen, that is, a family member with the duty to protect and help his own when they are in need.

Naomi speaks with Ruth, her daughter-in-law, who returned with her from Moab. Both are widows and poor. Ruth has just been gleaning, that is, gathering the ears of grain left behind by the reapers, and she arrives with a great deal of grain. Naomi, who had felt abandoned by God, now sees a sign of hope: God is still caring for them.

Today we can notice the small kindnesses we receive and recognize in them the hand of God, even in difficult times. And we can give thanks for them out loud, as Naomi did.
exp.1:22:
She stayed close to Boaz's young women, gleaning ears of grain, through the whole of the barley harvest and the wheat harvest. When the reaping ended, she went on living with her mother-in-law, Naomi. Gleaning means picking up the heads of grain that the reapers left behind. The young women are the girls who worked in the field, and to live with her means that she stayed under the same roof as her mother-in-law.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Ruth followed Naomi's advice not to go to other fields, where she might be in danger. The harvest lasted several weeks, and so Ruth had food for both of them. Israel's law allowed the poor and the foreigners to gather the grain left in the fields.

For today: Ruth was steadfast. She stayed in a safe place, listened to good counsel, and did not abandon her family. We can ask God for faithfulness in the ordinary details of each day, and surround ourselves with people who help us walk well.
exp.2:1:
Naomi reminds Ruth that Boaz is a relative of the family. Ruth had already worked alongside the young women who work for him. Now she tells her that tonight Boaz will be winnowing the barley, that is, tossing it into the air with a shovel so the wind separates the grain from the husk. The heap of grain and chaff is the pile left after the work, and the threshing floor is the flat ground where this work was done.

Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, is speaking. Both are widows and are in a difficult situation. Naomi looks for a secure home for Ruth and thinks of Boaz as a possible redeemer, a relative who could protect the family according to the law of Israel. The plan that follows belongs to that culture; today it is understood in several ways, but the text highlights Ruth's faithfulness.

For today: seek advice from wise people of faith, and act with respect and humility, trusting that God cares for you through the people He places in your path.
exp.2:2:
She says that Ruth should bathe, put oil on her body, and dress in her best clothes. Then she is to go down to the threshing floor, where the grain was beaten and winnowed. But she must not let Boaz see her until he has finished eating and drinking.

Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, is the one speaking. She is looking for a secure home for her widowed daughter-in-law. Boaz is a close relative of the family, and this points to his possible role as kinsman-redeemer. Scholars understand the exact purpose of this night-time plan in different ways, but the text shows that Ruth acts with respect and trust in Naomi's advice.

Today we can learn to listen humbly to wise and proven people, and to prepare with care and good timing when we take an important step, trusting that God is guiding us.
exp.2:3:
Here Naomi gives Ruth instructions. When Boaz lies down to sleep, she must take careful note of the place where he lies. Then she must go, uncover his feet, and lie down there. Afterward, Boaz will tell her what she is to do.

Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, speaks here. She seeks security for her daughter-in-law, who is a widow. Boaz is a close relative and could act as the family's redeemer under the law of Israel. This nighttime gesture is a custom little known today, and scholars understand it as a request for protection and marriage, made with respect. The text gives no further details.

For today: Ruth listens with humility and obeys the advice of a wise and trustworthy person. Let us seek counsel from people who are mature in faith, and then act with integrity and respect.
exp.2:4:
Ruth tells her mother-in-law Naomi that she will do everything Naomi tells her.

Ruth, a young widow from Moab, is the one speaking, and she is answering Naomi. Naomi is looking for a secure home for Ruth and wants Boaz, a close relative, to help her. The details of the plan were understood within the customs of that time, and some scholars interpret them in different ways. What is clear is that Ruth obeys with humility, and the following text shows that she carried out what was instructed.

Today we can learn to listen to the advice of wise and faithful people. Obeying with humility does not mean giving up thinking, but trusting and acting with respect, praying that God guides each step.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that Ruth went down to the threshing floor, which was the place where the grain was beaten out and winnowed, and that she did everything that Naomi, her mother-in-law, had told her to do. The words "so she went down to the threshing floor" mean that she went down to the place where Boaz was working with the barley harvest.

Naomi speaks in the verses before this one, and Ruth answers with obedience. Naomi is looking for a secure home for Ruth and, according to Israelite custom, Boaz could act as a kinsman-redeemer. Scholars understand in several ways what it meant to uncover the feet. The clearest reading is that Ruth was humbly asking for Boaz's protection.

For today: listening to the advice of wise and faithful people can help us greatly. Even so, it is good to act with respect, with prayer, and with integrity, as Ruth did.
exp.2:6:
Booz had finished eating and drinking, and he was in good spirits. Then he went to lie down at the far end of the heap of grain on the threshing floor. Ruth came quietly, uncovered his feet, and lay down there.

Naomi, her mother-in-law, had given Ruth these instructions. She wanted to secure a home and a future for her, since Boaz was a close relative who could redeem them. Uncovering the feet was a gesture that asked for protection, and Ruth did it with respect. Scholars debate some details of the custom, but the text presents Ruth as a woman of integrity, and Boaz treats her that way.

Today, Ruth teaches us to ask for help with humility and to trust wise counsel. Acting with respect and integrity, even in difficult situations, opens doors that God can use.
exp.2:7:
In the middle of the night, Boaz was startled, turned over, and there lying at his feet was a woman! He had been sleeping, and in the dark he found someone close to him he had not expected.

Context: The narrator tells what follows Naomi's plan. She wanted to secure the future of her daughter-in-law Ruth, and she sent her to ask Boaz, a close relative, to act as the family redeemer. Uncovering his feet and lying down there was a gesture of request and humility, according to the custom of that time. Some scholars debate the exact details of this act, but the text shows that Ruth acted with respect, and Boaz treated her with honor.

For today: When you face difficult decisions, seek wise counsel and act with integrity, trusting that God cares for you even in what is hidden.
exp.2:8:
Ruth tells Boaz her name, as he wakes up startled in the middle of the night. She presents herself as his servant, with humility. She asks him to spread his skirt over her, that is, to cover her with his protection. She reminds him that he is a near kinsman, someone with the right to redeem the family.

Ruth is a Moabite widow who lives with her mother-in-law, Naomi. Following Naomi's advice, she goes to the threshing floor where Boaz is working. Asking him to cover her with his skirt was a request for marriage and protection, according to many scholars. That custom belonged to that time. Boaz responds with kindness and respect, and does not take advantage of her.

For today: Ruth acted with humility and courage to seek what was right. When you need help, ask for it with honesty and respect. And if someone trusts you, care for them with integrity, as Boaz did.
exp.2:9:
Boaz tells Ruth that God blesses her. He calls her "my daughter" with affection. He says that her last act of kindness was better than her first. The young men are the youths, and she did not go after them, whether poor or rich.

Boaz speaks, an older man and a close relative of Naomi. Ruth, a widow and a foreigner, lay down at his feet and asked him to cover her with his cloak, a way of asking for protection and marriage. Many understand that her first act of kindness was her loyalty to Naomi, and the last, her desire to preserve the name of her late husband's family. Some interpret it in other ways.

Today we can choose what is right out of loyalty and character, not out of convenience or appearance. God sees those decisions and often uses faithful people to bless others.
exp.2:10:
Boaz tells Ruth not to be afraid. He commits himself to do what she asked. He explains that all the people of his town, that is, the people who gathered at the gate of the city, where public matters were handled, know that she is a woman of noble and strong character.

Ruth had come to Boaz at night, on the threshing floor, and asked him to spread his cloak over her, a gesture usually understood as a request for marriage and protection. Boaz, a close relative, praises her for her loyalty to Naomi. Even so, he makes clear that there is another relative with the first right.

For today: a good reputation is built through steady faithfulness in everyday life. Live with integrity even when no one sees you, and let your actions speak of your faith and your character.
exp.2:11:
Boaz tells Ruth that it is true he is a close relative of her family, and that for this reason he could marry her and provide protection for Naomi. But he makes clear that there is another relative with a prior right to hers over his own.

"Redeem" here means rescuing the family, caring for the widow, and keeping the name and land of the deceased.

Boaz speaks at night, on the threshing floor. Ruth has just asked him to act as a kinsman-redeemer. He praises her character, but he does not skip the order that the custom of his people required. He wants to do it properly and in the sight of all, without taking advantage of the situation.

For today: Boaz teaches us to be honest even when something would benefit us. If we want something good, we should seek it with integrity, respecting the limits and the people involved, and trusting that God guides the outcome.
exp.2:12:
Boaz tells Ruth to stay and sleep there that night. In the morning, if the closer relative is willing to do the duty of a kinsman for her, that is, to marry her and look after her family, then good, let him do it. If he is not willing, Boaz promises to do it himself, and he swears by the living Lord to keep his word.

Boaz is an older, respected man. Ruth, a widow and a foreigner, had come to him on Naomi's advice. Boaz acknowledges that there is a closer relative with the first right, and he wants to act in good order and honesty, protecting Ruth's reputation.

For today: do what is right in a fair and open way, even when no one is watching. Boaz does not take advantage of the situation. He respects Ruth, he respects the law, and he commits himself before God to keep his word.
exp.2:13:
She lay at his feet until morning, and she got up before anyone could recognize another person. Then Boaz said, "Let it not be known that a woman came into the threshing floor." The threshing floor was the place where the grain was beaten out and cleaned.

Here Boaz is speaking. Ruth had gone to him on Naomi's advice, seeking that he act as a kinsman-redeemer. Boaz wanted to protect her good name and his own, since a visit at night could be misunderstood. Scholars debate the exact details of the custom, but the text shows an upright man who protects Ruth.

For today: guarding our witness matters. Even when our intentions are good, it is wise to act with prudence and avoid situations that could give rise to misunderstanding. Integrity is also protected by wisdom.
exp.2:16:
Ruth tells Naomi what happened with Boaz. She shows her the barley and repeats what he said to her: that she should not go back to her mother-in-law with nothing in her hands.

Here Ruth is speaking, just back from the threshing floor, where she approached Boaz at night. Boaz gave her six measures of grain, though the text does not say exactly how much each measure was. His words about Naomi do not appear earlier in the story, so we do not know whether Ruth repeats them word for word or summarizes them. They show that Boaz had Naomi and her need in mind.

For today: God often takes care of those in need through generous people. Think of someone around you who is in need and share something concrete with them, without making them wait. You can also remember that your faithfulness to others may bring them a blessing.
exp.3:0:
This verse tells us that Boaz went up to the gate of the city and sat down there. Just then the close relative he had spoken about came by. Boaz called out to him: "Ho, such a one! Turn aside and sit down here." The text does not give the man's name, and he did as he was asked and sat down.

Here the narrator speaks, and then Boaz. In those days the city gate was the place where legal and public matters were settled. Boaz had promised Ruth that he would take up the matter of the relative who had the right to redeem the land of Elimelech, before he himself would do so. That is why he acts in an orderly way and in full view of everyone.

For today: when you have to settle something important, do it with patience, honesty, and openness, without shortcuts. Boaz did not rush or act in secret; he sought to do things properly.
exp.3:2:
Boaz tells the kinsman that Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling a parcel of land that belonged to Elimelech, a relative of them both. The word "kinsman" here refers to a close relative who has the right to redeem, that is, to buy the land so that it would not leave the family.

Boaz speaks at the city gate, where legal matters were settled, and he does so before ten elders as witnesses. He wants to carry out, in an orderly and honest way, what is due to Naomi and Ruth. Scholars discuss the exact details of this custom, but it is understood that the family was to protect the widow and the inheritance.

For today: when you have to help someone in need, do it with clarity and uprightness, without shortcuts or secrets. Caring for the vulnerable also means acting with transparency and respect.
exp.3:4:
Boaz tells the relative that, on the same day he buys the fields from Naomi, he must also take Ruth the Moabitess, the widow of the dead man, as his wife. So "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" means that the first son would carry on the memory and the inheritance of Elimelech's family.

Boaz speaks before the elders, at the city gate. According to the law of Israel, a close relative could redeem the family's land and care for the widow. Boaz does not hide the condition: the full truth leaves the relative to decide with clear eyes. Some scholars debate how this relates to the laws of redemption and levirate marriage.

For today: when it falls to you to help or to decide, be honest and do not hide what it costs. Loving someone truly sometimes means commitment, not just gain.
exp.3:6:
In this verse the narrator describes an old custom in Israel. When someone redeemed a property or made an agreement, a person would take off his shoe and give it to the other person to confirm the deal. This served as a public sign that the agreement was valid. Redeeming refers to getting back what the family had lost, and a matter is a deal or business arrangement.

Here the narrator speaks to the reader, explaining the custom. Naomi's closest relative gives up his right to buy back the land of Elimelech, and Boaz is free to do so and to marry Ruth. The shoe was the testimony before the elders. The full symbolism of the shoe is not known with certainty; many think it represented the right to walk on or possess the land.

For today: when you promise something, keep your word clearly and in full view of others. Integrity and openness in agreements protect people and honor God.
exp.3:8:
Boaz speaks before the elders and all the people, and asks them to be witnesses. He declares that he is acquiring everything that had belonged to Elimelech, to Chilion, and to Mahlon, that is, the inheritance of Naomi's family.

We are at the city gate, where legal matters were settled. Another relative closer in line gave up his right to redeem the land, and the sandal was the public sign of that arrangement. Boaz acts as the family's redeemer, and so he protects both Naomi and Ruth.

For today: Boaz acted with clarity, in full view of everyone, and kept his word. We can follow his example by being trustworthy in our commitments and by caring for those who need protection.
exp.3:9:
Boaz publicly announces that he is taking Ruth, the Moabitess, as his wife. She was the widow of Mahlon, son of Naomi. He says he does this "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance," that is, so that Mahlon's name would not be cut off and would continue on his family's land. He also asks everyone present to be witnesses.

Boaz speaks before the elders and the people gathered at the gate of Bethlehem. Another relative, closer in kinship, had given up his right to redeem the land and to marry Ruth. In this way Boaz, openly and within the law, fulfills the duty of the kinsman-redeemer and protects the memory and the inheritance of Elimelech's family.

For today: Boaz keeps his word with integrity and cares for someone who was vulnerable. We can ask ourselves whom we might protect or serve today, doing what is right with honesty and without seeking applause.
exp.3:12:
This verse tells us that Boaz took Ruth as his wife, and she became his wife. Then the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son. The verse describes their marriage and the child's birth plainly, as the work of the LORD in their lives.

The narrator of the book recounts what happened after the wedding. Shortly before, the people and the elders at the city gate, where legal matters were settled, had witnessed the agreement and blessed Boaz. Afterward, the women will praise God together with Naomi, because her family was no longer left without descendants or without protection.

For today: God can faithfully care for us in the midst of loss and emptiness. We can trust that He works in everyday life, and we can also be, like Boaz, people who help and protect those who are in need.
exp.3:15:
She says that Naomi took the newborn child, laid him in her lap, that is, on her knees, close to her breast, and became his nurse. "Nurse" here means the one who cares for and attends to the child, like a nanny or a wet nurse. The text does not make clear whether she nursed him; what is certain is that she took on the task of raising him with tenderness.

The one acting is Naomi, a woman who had lost her husband and her two sons. The women of Bethlehem had just told her that God had given her a restorer for her life. This child, Obed, was born to Ruth and Boaz, and would later become the grandfather of King David.

For today: God can restore meaning and joy after a great loss. We can open our arms to the new things He places in our lives and serve with love those who come after us.
exp.3:16:
The neighbour women, seeing the baby, said, "A son has been born to Naomi," and they gave him the name Obed. The text notes that Obed was the father of Jesse, and that Jesse was the father of David.

The story comes after Boaz married Ruth. It is the women who speak, and they rejoice that Naomi, who had lost her husband and her sons, now has a family and a future. The narrator adds the mention of David to show how God cared for two widows and, at the same time, continued a line that would lead to the king of Israel. Some scholars discuss why it was the neighbour women who gave the name, since this was not the usual custom.

For today: God can work in the midst of loss and through ordinary people. Stay faithful in small things, because He can use them for something greater than you can see.
exp.2:0:
Naomi speaks to her daughter-in-law Ruth with warmth. She calls her "my daughter" and asks whether she should not seek a resting place for her, meaning a secure and stable home, something that will be good for her. The question "should I not seek a resting place for you" is worded in a way that may sound formal to modern ears. In this context, rest is understood as security and well-being, probably through marriage.

Naomi is a widow, and so is Ruth. Both returned from Moab to Bethlehem, and they live on what Ruth gathers in the fields. Naomi thinks about Ruth's future and sees in Boaz, a relative, a possibility. Commentators explain the customs that appear later in different ways, but here the sincere concern of Naomi is clear.

For today: caring about the well-being of others is a form of love. We can ask ourselves whom we might help with wise counsel, practical support, or prayer, always seeking what will truly do them good.
exp.0:4:
This verse tells that Mahlon and Chilion, Naomi's two sons, also died. So Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband. The phrase "without protection" describes the situation: she had no one to provide for her or care for her.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. He shows us Naomi's darkest moment: she was a foreigner in Moab and a widow without children, something very hard in that time, when a woman depended on her family. This grief leads her to decide to return to Judah, where God had given bread to his people.

For today: when life leaves you without support, do not hide your pain. Naomi truly suffered, but even so she set out on the road back. Take the next step toward God and toward trusted people.
exp.1:11:
Boaz prays that the LORD would repay Ruth for all the good she has done. He asks that she would receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel. The picture of being sheltered under God's wings is one of care and protection, like a bird that covers its young.

Boaz speaks with Ruth, a young woman from Moab. She left her family and her homeland to stay with her mother-in-law Naomi, who, like her, was a widow. Ruth was gleaning in Boaz's field to find food. He has heard of her loyalty, and he blesses her, recognizing her courage and her faith in the God of Israel.

God sees the quiet sacrifices we make out of love and faith. We can trust that he cares for those who take refuge in him. And like Boaz, we can encourage those who struggle in silence with words of blessing.
exp.3:5:
Here the nearest relative of Naomi says he cannot redeem the land. "Redeem" means buying back a family property so that it is not lost. The phrase "I would jeopardize my own inheritance" means that he would put his own estate at risk. That is why he gives up his right to Boaz.

The relative speaks before the elders at the city gate. At first he agreed to buy the land, but Boaz added that he must also marry Ruth, to raise up offspring for the deceased. With that condition, the relative drew back. The text does not explain his fear precisely; it is usually thought that it would affect his inheritance or his finances.

For today: serving others has a cost, and it is worth thinking about honestly. Boaz shows us the way of generous love, which cares for the vulnerable without clinging to one's own interests.
exp.2:17:
Naomi tells Ruth to stay calm and wait until she sees how things turn out. In her view, Boaz will not rest until he settles the matter today. "Until you find out how things go" means until you see how the matter ends, and "resolved the matter" refers to the arrangement still pending.

Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, is the one speaking. Ruth has just come back from the threshing floor, where Boaz gave her six measures of barley and showed his goodwill toward her. Naomi knows that Boaz, as a close relative, could act as the family's redeemer, and so she trusts that he will move the matter forward soon. Another relative who is closer still is pending, as will be seen later.

For today: after doing what is yours to do with wisdom and honesty, learn to wait in peace. Resting is not doing nothing, but trusting that God is also at work while you wait.
exp.3:1:
Boaz takes ten of the elders, that is, the respected leaders of the city, and asks them to sit here at the city gate. They do as he asks. The instruction "sit here" is a simple, courteous request.

Boaz wants to settle the matter of Naomi and Ruth in the right way. In that time, the city gate was the place where legal matters were handled. The ten elders would serve as public witnesses. Boaz does not want to act in secret or take advantage of his position, but to do everything with order and openness.

For today: when you have to make an important decision, act with honesty and in the open. Seek wise counsel and let others see what you do, so that your conduct is clear and fair.
exp.1:3:
This verse tells how Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and greeted his harvesters with the words: "The LORD be with you." They answered him: "The LORD bless you." The name "LORD" stands for God, and "harvesters" are the workers who cut the grain at harvest time. "Just then" points to the moment his arrival follows what has just happened.

Boaz is a wealthy man of the town, a relative of Elimelech, the late husband of Naomi. Ruth, a young woman from Moab, had gone out to gather the heads of grain left behind after the harvest, to provide for Naomi and herself. The text says she happened to arrive at his field, and many readers see in this the quiet hand of God. This greeting shows the character of Boaz and the atmosphere of respect in his field.

For today: we can begin our work and our relationships with a sincere blessing. A kind greeting that invokes God can create an atmosphere of respect and care.
exp.1:2:
Ruth set out and came to the field, and began gathering the grain stalks left behind by the harvesters. "Gleaning" means collecting the stalks that fall or are left after the harvest. The verse says she happened to come to that part of the field, meaning she arrived there by chance; the phrase "the part of the field" refers to a particular plot of land.

It turned out to be the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech, the late husband of Naomi.

The narrator tells us that Ruth, a Moabite widow, went out to find food for herself and her mother-in-law. The law of Moses left the gleanings for the poor and for foreigners (Leviticus 19:9-10). What seems to be chance, the text does not fully explain; many readers see here the quiet hand of God, though God's name does not appear in this verse.

For today: do with diligence whatever lies within your reach, even if it is something humble, and trust that God may be guiding your steps even in the "chances" you do not understand.
exp.1:5:
The foreman answers and says that the young woman gleaning in the field is the Moabite woman who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab. In the verse, he identifies her as the Moabitess who came back with Naomi from the land of Moab.

The foreman speaks, answering Boaz's question, "Whose young woman is this?" Boaz had just arrived from Bethlehem and noticed a stranger. Notice that the foreman does not introduce her by her name, but by her origin and by her loyalty to Naomi. Ruth was a foreigner, and yet her faithfulness was already known and respected.

For today: the way we live speaks about us even when no one knows us. Strive to be steady and loyal in small things, because God uses that to open doors and to win the respect of others.
exp.3:11:
The people say they want the children that the LORD gives Boaz through Ruth to build a strong family, like the family of Perez, the son Tamar bore to Judah. "Offspring" means descendants, "young woman" refers to Ruth, and "bore" means gave birth.

The ones speaking are the elders and the people gathered at the city gate, where legal matters were settled. They have just witnessed Boaz marrying Ruth, the Moabite, in order to keep alive the name of her late husband. Perez was an ancestor of Judah and well known in Bethlehem. His story, like Ruth's, shows that God works even in difficult situations.

For today: We can bless families who are just beginning by praying that God will sustain them and make them a blessing to many.
exp.0:2:
This verse tells, briefly and directly, that Naomi's husband Elimelech died in a foreign land. Naomi was left a widow, but not alone: she still had her two sons with her. In this wording, the phrase "she was left with her two sons" means that her sons were still with her after the loss.

The one who speaks is the narrator of the book of Ruth. He tells the story of a family from Bethlehem who left their land because of famine and went to Moab, in the time of the judges. The death of Elimelech is the first painful blow in a series of losses that prepares the way for what God will do later in the lives of Naomi and Ruth.

For today: when losses come that we did not expect, we are not outside God's care. We can grieve honestly, lean on those who walk with us, and trust that God is still at work, even when we cannot yet see how.
exp.3:10:
All the people who were at the city gate, along with the elders, said, "We are witnesses." Then they prayed that the Lord would make the woman entering Boaz's home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. They also wished that Boaz would prosper, and that he would be famous in Ephrathah and in Bethlehem.

Context: Boaz had just declared publicly that he was buying the land that belonged to Elimelech and that he was marrying Ruth, the Moabite, to preserve the name of her late husband. The gate was the place where legal matters were settled, and that is why the people spoke as witnesses and gave their blessing.

For today: Blessing others from the heart, even those who come from outside, helps build welcoming communities. We can pray for the new families in our church or neighborhood.
exp.0:10:
Naomi again asks her daughters-in-law to go back to their own homes. She asks them why they would want to go with her, since there are no more sons she could give them as husbands.

Naomi speaks after losing her husband and her two sons in Moab. Now she is returning to Bethlehem, and her daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, want to go with her. In that time, a widow without children had little future. Naomi thinks about their wellbeing and speaks to them frankly, even though she is full of sorrow.

For today: loving someone truly sometimes means thinking of the other person's good, even when it hurts to be left alone. It also teaches us to speak with honesty and tenderness, and not to manipulate those we love with our pain.
exp.3:18:
It says that Hezron was the father of Ram, and Ram was the father of Amminadab. "Was the father of" simply means that one man is the parent of the next name in the list. It is part of a list of ancestors, from Perez down to David.

The narrator of the book of Ruth closes the story with this family line. After telling how Naomi, Ruth and Boaz were cared for by God, he shows that Ruth's son, Obed, became the grandfather of King David. Ruth was a Moabite, that is, a foreigner, and yet she appears in David's line. Some scholars note that lists like this can summarize many generations, so they do not always mention everyone. Christians also see here a path that leads to Jesus, according to Matthew 1.

For today: even if your name does not appear in the great stories, God can use your faithful and simple life for a greater purpose. Serve him steadily today, trusting that he sees what you do not yet see.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that Obed was the father of Jesse, and that Jesse was the father of David. The phrase "was the father of" is repeated in the link from one name to the next. Finally, the book of Ruth ends with a family list.

The narrator closes the story of Ruth and Boaz by showing where everything led. Ruth was a Moabite, a foreigner, and yet she became the grandmother of Jesse and the great-grandmother of King David. This genealogy shows that God cared for an ordinary woman and worked in her story toward something much greater. Scholars generally agree that the book wants to connect this story with the origins of Israel's royal house.

For today: God can use lives that seem small, hidden, or difficult. Be faithful in everyday things, even when you cannot see the result, and trust that God is still writing your story.
exp.0:19:
Naomi asks the women of Bethlehem not to call her Naomi, which means "my sweetness" or "my pleasantness," but to call her Mara, which means "bitterness." She says that the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with her, filling her life with great hardship.

Naomi speaks as she returns to Bethlehem after years in Moab. There she lost her husband and her two sons. The women are astonished to see her, and she expresses her pain with honesty. It is clear that she attributes her suffering to God, although the book will go on to show that He was still working on her behalf.

For today: when you suffer, you do not need to pretend that you are fine. You can tell God honestly what you feel, as Naomi did. Even so, keep walking toward the place where He can restore you.
exp.0:17:
Ruth 1:18 tells us that Naomi realized Ruth was fully determined to go with her. So Naomi stopped trying to persuade her to turn back. The word "determined" means Ruth was firm in her decision, and "go with her" means exactly that: to go along with Naomi.

Naomi was a widow returning to Bethlehem from Moab, after losing her husband and her two sons. She had already urged Ruth and Orpah to go back to their own families. Orpah said goodbye, but Ruth stayed and pledged her loyalty to Naomi and to Naomi's God. The narrator sums up the end of that conversation here.

For today: when a person makes a firm and good decision out of love and faithfulness, their commitment often speaks louder than many words. We can also learn to recognize when to stop insisting and to respect someone's sincere conviction.
exp.1:7:
Boaz speaks to Ruth kindly and tells her to listen. He asks her not to go and glean in another field or to leave this place, but to stay close to his servant girls. "Glean" means to gather the heads of grain that are left behind after the harvest. The "servant girls" are the young women who worked for him.

Boaz is the owner of the field. Ruth is a widow from Moab who came with her mother-in-law Naomi, and she went out to glean so that both of them could eat. After hearing from the servant how hard she had been working, Boaz offers her protection, a safe place, and provision. Later she is amazed to receive such kindness as a foreigner.

Today we can learn to be generous and to care for those who are in need or who feel out of place. A concrete action might be to welcome someone new in your church, workplace, or neighborhood, and to offer them help and companionship.
exp.3:19:
It says that Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, and that Nahshon was the father of Salmon. The word "father" here means the direct father of each man. In biblical genealogies, "father" can sometimes mean an ancestor, so some skipping of generations is possible.

The author of Ruth closes the book with this family list, which runs from Perez, son of Judah, down to David. Nahshon appears in Numbers as a leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness. Salmon was the father of Boaz, Ruth's husband. In this way, the story of a foreign widow and a generous man is joined to God's larger plan for Israel.

For today: God works in ordinary lives, across generations. You may not see the result of your faithfulness, but God does see it. Be faithful today in small things, trusting that He can use them for something greater.
exp.0:18:
So Naomi and Ruth traveled until they came to Bethlehem. When they entered Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women of the town exclaimed, "Can this be Naomi?" The town was stirred up at the sight of them, and the women were so surprised that they could hardly recognize her.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. Years earlier, Naomi had left Bethlehem with her husband and sons because of a famine. Now she was returning as a widow, without her sons and marked by grief. Ruth, her Moabite daughter-in-law, had promised to stay at her side. That is why the people were surprised: the woman who left with her family came back changed and almost alone.

When life changes us through suffering, we do not need to pretend we are fine. Naomi returned honestly, and God did not reject her. Moreover, He placed Ruth at her side. Today we can come back to God just as we are, and let others walk with us.
exp.1:1:
Ruth, the woman from Moab, asks Naomi if she may go into the fields and gather heads of grain, meaning the grain left behind after the harvesters have passed. She hopes to glean after someone in whose sight she may find favor. Naomi answers her warmly: "Go ahead, my daughter."

Ruth and Naomi are widows and poor, newly arrived in Bethlehem. The law of Moses allowed the poor and foreigners to gather what was left in the fields (Leviticus 19:9-10). Ruth, who is not an Israelite, takes the initiative to find food for both of them. The text goes on to say that she arrived at the field of Boaz, and it does not explain beyond that how this came about.

For today: when you are in need, do not stay frozen in place. Take a humble step and work with what you have, trusting that God can open doors in unexpected ways.
exp.2:14:
Here Boaz asks Ruth to bring the shawl she is wearing and hold it out. He pours in six measures of barley, places it on her, and she goes back into the city.

The verse below is for you to read as your guide to this verse. The Hebrew text has some uncertainty about who goes into the city, so this is a point worth keeping in mind as you read.

Boaz speaks. Ruth had gone to the threshing floor at night, following Naomi's advice, to ask him to act as a kinsman-redeemer. Boaz promises to look after her, but he also wants to protect the reputation of both of them. That is why he sends her home with the barley before dawn. We do not know for certain how much the six measures weighed, since the text does not specify the unit.

For today: Boaz shows that generosity and integrity go together. We can help others with concrete gifts and, at the same time, protect their dignity and good name, acting with discretion and respect.
exp.0:3:
This verse tells us that Naomi's two sons, Mahlon and Chilion, married Moabite women: Orpah and Ruth. "Took Moabite women as their wives" simply means that they got married. "After they had lived in Moab about ten years" means that the family stayed in Moab for about ten years.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book, who presents the events in a simple way. The family had gone to Moab because of a famine in Judah. The husband had died, and now the sons were setting up their own homes. The text does not explain whether there were problems over marrying foreign women; it only reports. This is where Ruth first appears, and she will be very important in the story.

For today: God can work in the middle of situations we do not understand or that seem far from ideal. Even in times of loss and change, He continues to guide the story. Trust Him and stay attentive to what He is doing.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that the newborn child will be the one who gives Naomi back her will to live and who will care for her when she is old. "Renew your life" means someone who brings fresh life and spirit. "Sustain you in your old age" means that he will support and care for her in her later years. "Has given him birth" means that Ruth gave birth to him. Ruth, your daughter-in-law, loves you and is better to you than seven sons.

The women of Bethlehem are speaking. Naomi had returned from Moab a widow, without husband or children, and bitter over her loss. Now, with the birth of Obed, they celebrate that her family continues. Seven was a number of fullness, so they praise Ruth highly. The book ends by connecting Obed with David.

For today: value and express gratitude to those who stand by you faithfully, and trust that God can restore hope after a great loss.
exp.0:5:
This verse tells how Naomi decided to leave Moab and return to her own land with her two daughters-in-law. The reason was that she heard the Lord had attended to His people by providing them with food, meaning that God had cared for Israel and given them food again. Here "attended to" means to look after and help with care.

This is the voice of the narrator of the book of Ruth. Naomi is a widow who lost her husband and her two sons in a foreign land. At first she had left Judah because of a famine. Now, alone and in great sorrow, she hears news of provision and decides to go back.

For today: when you are in a time of loss or emptiness, do not just stay looking at your pain. Take a step toward where you know God is at work, even if the steps are small and your heart is tired.
exp.3:3:
Boaz tells the closest relative that he wants to let him know about something important. He asks him to decide, in the presence of those seated here and the elders of the people, whether he wants to buy back the land of Elimelech, that is, purchase it so that it does not pass out of the family. If he will not redeem it, he should say so, so Boaz can know, because Boaz is next in line after him. The man answers: "I will redeem it."

Boaz speaks at the city gate, where legal matters were settled. Naomi, a widow and poor, needed a kinsman-redeemer, a relative who would protect the family's inheritance. Boaz respects the proper order and does not take advantage, even though he wants to marry Ruth. What follows in the story shows that the matter was more complicated.

For today: act with honesty and openness, even when a shortcut would benefit you. Boaz did what was right, in full view of everyone, and trusted that God would take care of the outcome.
exp.1:20:
Here Ruth tells Naomi what Boaz said to her in the field. He invited her to stay close to his young men, his workers, until they had finished gathering all his harvest. The word "glean" means gathering the heads of grain left behind after the reapers.

Ruth is a foreign widow, from Moab, who cares for her mother-in-law Naomi. She tells with enthusiasm how Boaz treated her well. Naomi recognizes that Boaz is a close relative, a "kinsman-redeemer," someone who according to the law could help the family. So she advises her to stay in that field, where she will be protected.

For today: God often cares for us through people and safe places. When someone offers us help and protection with good intentions, let us learn to receive it with humility, and seek also to be that kind of support for others.
exp.1:15:
They say that the workers should not only let Ruth gather the stalks of grain, but should even pull out some stalks from the bundles for her and leave them for her to gather. The phrase "pull out for her" means to take out on purpose, with intention. "Leave them for her to gather" means that she may pick them up, and "do not rebuke her" means that they should not scold her or bother her.

Boaz, the owner of the field, is speaking to his servants who are harvesting. Ruth was a foreign widow from Moab, who was gleaning to feed her mother-in-law Naomi. The law of Moses already required leaving grain for the poor and the foreigner (Leviticus 19:9-10), but Boaz goes beyond the minimum. He gives her protection, dignity, and abundance.

For today: it is not enough to do the bare minimum when helping others. We can give generously and care for the dignity of the one in need, so that they do not feel humiliated, but respected and blessed.
exp.1:0:
This verse introduces a new character: Boaz. It says that Naomi had a relative on her husband Elimelech's side, and that he was a prominent man of noble character. The phrase "a prominent man of noble character" describes a man of good standing, capable and respected. Some understand it to refer to his wealth, others to his character and worth. It probably includes both.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Naomi and Ruth had just returned from Moab to Bethlehem, widows with no means of support. The author introduces Boaz before Ruth meets him, as one who prepares the way. Afterward, Ruth goes out to gather grain, and the text says that she happened to come to the field of Boaz. Many readers see in this the hand of God working quietly.

For today: God often acts in ordinary things, even when we do not notice. If you are in a time of need, keep faithfully doing what is in front of you, and trust that God may be preparing help that you cannot yet see.
exp.1:9:
Ruth bows low, with her face to the ground, and asks Boaz why she has found such favor (that is, kindness and good treatment) in his eyes, since she is a foreigner. The phrase "take notice of me" means that he would see her and give her attention. Ruth did not expect this.

Ruth is speaking. She is a Moabite widow who came to Bethlehem with her mother-in-law Naomi. Boaz has just offered her protection and water in his field. She is surprised because, being a foreigner and poor, she had no right to expect such kindness. Boaz replies that he already knows of her loyalty to Naomi.

For today: God often shows his goodness through generous people. We can receive the help of others with humility and gratitude, and also notice those who feel like outsiders or unseen, so that we treat them with respect and care.
exp.2:15:
Ruth returned to her mother-in-law, Naomi, and Naomi asked her, "How did it go, my daughter?" Ruth then told her everything that Boaz had done for her.

Naomi had advised Ruth to go at night to the threshing floor and approach Boaz, a relative who could redeem them. This was a respectful request for protection and marriage, according to the custom of the time. Naomi waited eagerly for the answer, since her future and Ruth's depended on it. Ruth tells her everything with confidence and without hiding anything.

For today: when you need direction, seek out a wise and faithful person, and tell them your situation with sincerity. Good counsel grows stronger when there is trust and honesty.
exp.1:21:
Naomi tells Ruth, her daughter-in-law, that it is good for her to go out and work with Boaz's young women, so that nothing will happen to her in another field, where she might be harmed. The words "so that nothing will happen to you" suggest that the danger is real, and the young women who worked for Boaz were a place where Ruth would be safer.

Naomi speaks as an older widow who knows the customs of the region. Ruth is a foreigner, a widow, and poor, and she was gleaning so that both of them would have something to eat. Naomi recognizes the kindness of Boaz, who is a close relative, and cares for Ruth with a mother's wisdom. The text does not spell out the dangers, but it suggests that a woman alone could face risks.

For today: it is wise to accept the advice of people with experience and to seek places and companies that protect us. God often cares for us through others, and listening with humility can keep us from problems we cannot see.
exp.0:16:
Ruth tells Naomi that she will not leave her side. Where you die, I will die, and there I want to be buried. She says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely," an ancient oath formula that means: "may God punish me if I do not keep my word." Only death will separate them.

The speaker is Ruth, a young Moabite widow. Naomi, also a widow and without sons, returns to Bethlehem and tries to persuade her daughters-in-law to go back to their families. Orpah goes back, but Ruth stays. By making this vow in the name of the LORD, Ruth leaves her people and her gods and joins Naomi and her God.

For today: true loyalty shows itself in difficult moments. Think of someone who is suffering or alone today, and stand with them through a phone call, a visit, or concrete help, without expecting anything in return.
exp.1:4:
Boaz asks the foreman of his harvesters, "Whose young woman is this?" The word "foreman" means the person in charge of the workers and supervising the work, and "young woman" means a girl or a young woman. Whose is a plain way of asking who someone belongs to or what family they come from.

Boaz, a landowner who has just arrived from Bethlehem, greets his workers with a blessing. Ruth, a foreign widow from Moab, is gleaning, that is, gathering the heads of grain that the reapers leave behind. The Law allowed the poor and foreigners to do this. Boaz notices a stranger and takes an interest in her. The text does not say what he thought at that moment.

For today: notice the people who go unnoticed, especially those who are alone or new. Asking with genuine interest can open the door to helping.
exp.1:18:
Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, asks her where she gathered grain today and where she worked. Seeing how much barley Ruth has brought home, Naomi concludes that someone was kind to her, and she blesses that person. The word "gleaned" means gathering the grain left behind in the field after the harvesters. "Noticed you" means that he saw her and treated her with kindness. Ruth tells Naomi where she worked and gives the man's name: Boaz.

Naomi and Ruth are poor widows who have returned from Moab to Bethlehem. Ruth went out to glean so that the two of them would have food. Naomi speaks with emotion because she sees God's provision. She does not yet know who the man is, and when she hears the name Boaz she recognizes that he is a close relative of the family.

For today: when someone helps you, acknowledge their kindness and give thanks. And if God sustains you through a difficult season, tell others so that they too may praise him.
exp.1:16:
Ruth kept gathering grain in the field until evening. When she beat out what she had gathered, she ended up with about an ephah of barley. "Gathering" here means collecting the grain the harvesters leave behind. An "ephah" was a measure of volume; many estimate it at around 20 to 22 liters, though the exact calculation is debated. That would have been roughly 14 to 16 kilos of grain.

Here the narrator speaks. Ruth is a foreign widow who cares for her mother-in-law Naomi. Boaz, the owner of the field, had ordered his workers to treat her with respect and even to let grain fall on purpose. That is why her labor yielded so much.

For today: God often cares for us through steady work and through generous people. Do your part with energy, even if it is humble, and give thanks for those who help you. If you can, be that help to someone else.
exp.3:13:
Here the women of Bethlehem speak to Naomi and bless the Lord because she has not been left without a family redeemer. That redeemer is the newborn child, who will restore the family. They say his name will be made famous in Israel. The blessing is directed to the Lord, and the name the verse looks to is his son's name.

The ones speaking are Naomi's neighbors. She had returned from Moab a widow, without children, with a bitter heart. Now, through Ruth's marriage to Boaz, a son is born who gives the family a future and someone to carry on its line. The women recognize that God brought about this change. The child's name, Obed, appears shortly afterward, and the book connects him with the line of David.

For today: when someone goes through a time of emptiness or pain, stand beside them as these women did. And when God gives you something good, do not keep it quiet: give thanks out loud and share the joy with others.
exp.3:20:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Salmon was the father of Boaz, and that Boaz was the father of Obed. The word "father" here means that Salmon had a son who was Boaz, and Boaz had a son who was Obed. In this period, the list does not always name every descendant, and some scholars think it may summarize several generations.

The book of Ruth ends with this genealogy, written by an author who is not named. Its purpose is to show that Boaz, the redeemer who married Ruth, the foreigner from Moab, was part of the path that led to King David. Thus the story of a simple family is joined to God's plan for his people. The New Testament also includes Boaz and Ruth in the line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

For today: God can use lives that seem small and quiet to fulfill great purposes. Be faithful in everyday things, because your obedience may bless generations you do not yet know.
exp.3:7:
Here the closest relative says to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," meaning, "you take my place." To confirm this, he removes his sandal. The sandal is what he removed, and the nearest relative with the right to redeem is the one who does this.

The closest relative of Elimelech had hesitated to redeem Naomi's land, because doing so included marrying Ruth and would affect his own inheritance. Boaz, however, was willing. Handing over the sandal was then a public sign that confirmed the deal before the elders, at the gate of the city. In this way Boaz was free to act as the family's redeemer.

Today, Boaz shows us that truly loving someone sometimes costs something and demands commitment. Think of someone who needs your help or your firm word, and ask yourself whether you are willing to take on that responsibility, as Christ, our Redeemer, took on ours.
exp.3:17:
This verse begins a family list. It says that Perez, son of Judah, was the father of Hezron. The phrase "the generations of" refers to a person's descendants or family history. The name is spelled Perez in your Bible.

The narrator of the book closes the story of Ruth with this family line. We do not know for certain who wrote the book. After telling of the birth of Obed, it traces this family down to David. In this way we see that God cared for Ruth and Naomi, and used their lives for something much greater. Ruth was a foreigner, and yet she appears within this line.

For today: do not underestimate your daily life or your small acts of faithfulness. You may not see all that God is doing, but He can use your obedience and your kindness to bless future generations.
exp.0:14:
Naomi tells Ruth that her sister-in-law Orpah has already gone back to her own people, to Moab, and to her gods. She urges Ruth to do the same and follow Orpah back home.

Speaking is Naomi, an Israelite widow who lost her husband and both of her sons in a foreign land. She wants to return to Bethlehem and believes her daughters-in-law will be better off with their own families. Her grief is deep, and she feels that God has dealt harshly with her. Some think she is testing Ruth's faith, others that she only seeks to protect them. The Bible does not make this clear.

For today: when others offer us an easy way out, we can ask ourselves what is right and faithful. Ruth chose to stay, to love, and to trust in Naomi's God, even without guarantees.
exp.0:20:
Naomi says that she left Bethlehem full, with a husband and sons, but that the LORD brought her back empty. She asks why they call her Naomi, a name that means "pleasant" or "my pleasantness," if she feels that the LORD has turned against her. The phrase "testified against me" sounds like an accusation or a sentence. "Afflicted" means to cause someone suffering. "Almighty" translates the Hebrew name Shaddai.

Naomi speaks this on her return to Bethlehem, after being widowed and losing her two sons in Moab. The women of the town recognize her, and she expresses her bitterness to them. She does not yet see what God will do. Ruth is at her side, and the story is only beginning, with the barley harvest.

Today we can speak to God honestly in our pain, without pretending that we are fine. Naomi complains, but she keeps returning to God's place and to his people. And God may already be at work, even though we cannot yet see it.

sum.2: Naomi advises Ruth to go to the threshing floor at night and lie down at the feet of Boaz, and she does as she is told. Boaz praises her as a woman of noble character, promises to act as her redeemer, and tells her there is a closer relative. He gives her six measures of barley, and Naomi asks Ruth to wait patiently.
sum.1: Ruth went out to glean in a field and, without planning it, ended up in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi. Boaz took care of her, gave her food and water, and praised her loyalty to her mother-in-law. Naomi saw in this the kindness of God, and Ruth kept working there until the harvest was finished.
sum.3: Boaz meets with the nearest relative and the elders at the city gate. Since the relative gives up his right to redeem the land, Boaz buys it and marries Ruth. God gives them a son, Obed, who brings joy to Naomi and becomes the grandfather of King David.
sum.0: Because of the famine, Naomi went to Moab with her family, but there her husband and her two sons died. When she heard that God had given bread to his people, she returned to Bethlehem. Her daughter-in-law Ruth, determined not to leave her, promised her: "Your people will be my people, and your God my God." Naomi arrived bitter, but just at the beginning of the barley harvest.
